1:
The command is read backwards, against the chapter before it. Clarke takes it as a conclusion drawn from what precedes: the Judaizing teachers not only taught a false doctrine but led an unholy life, and Titus was to act directly opposite, proclaiming a sacred doctrine and the things which become it, so that principle and practice go hand in hand. Ellicott makes the same contrast govern the whole chapter. Titus' first work in Crete had been organisation; his second and equally weighty mission was the refutation of a school of professed Christian teachers who were fatally lowering the tone of Christian life by their example, and it is that moral influence rather than the doctrinal error to which his attention is especially directed — which is why the charges are so remarkably practical, a quiet and useful life pressed home upon every age and rank before doctrine is touched at all. The phrase itself, Ellicott adds, is peculiar to these Pastoral Epistles and stands in clear contrast to the sickly and fanciful teaching of the misleading men in Crete.

Calvin takes the metaphor in earnest. Doctrine is called sound from the effect produced by it: it means wholesome, that which actually feeds souls, and so serves not only for nourishment but for medicine, since we are full of vices which are worse than diseases. He presses the comparison to an uncomfortable end — when we want food for the body we are immediately terrified and have not a moment of repose, because it touches us nearly, while we are insensible to all that affects our souls; and he divides sound doctrine into two parts, the one magnifying the grace of God in Christ so that we learn where to seek salvation, the other framing the life to the fear of God. Henry keeps the charge on Titus himself: ordaining others to preach would not excuse him from preaching, nor might he take care of ministers and elders only, and ministers must not stay in generals but divide to every one his portion, which is why what follows is an excellent Christian directory accommodated to each age and condition.

On the aged men the voices converge and then part. Barnes rests the identification on the word, an unusual noun occurring nowhere else in the New Testament except twice, once in a gospel and once of Paul the aged, and in no instance applied to an office; Ellicott says simply the old men in the congregations, Clarke that the whole context requires the literal sense, and Henry reports that some understand elders by office, including deacons, before taking it of the aged in point of years. The parting is over what sobriety asks of them. Clarke keeps it concrete, quoting Seneca that a young man addicted to luxury transgresses while an old man thus addicted runs mad; Ellicott wants a more extended sense than the bare literal meaning would give, the elder men thoughtful in contrast with the thoughtlessness of careless youth. Chrysostom supplies the reason such an exhortation is needed at all, since age has failings that youth has not — a slowness, a timidity, a forgetfulness, an insensibility, an irritability — and among the old some rave and are beside themselves, some from wine and some from sorrow, for old age makes them narrowminded. Hence the last word is the fitting one. Ellicott observes that patience here takes the place of hope in the familiar Pauline three, because enduring fortitude especially becomes the old man waiting for death; Barnes turns it toward the infirmities of advanced years and the loss of the friends of early ones, and says that a few more sighs and they will sigh no more.
3:
The question of office recurs and is answered differently. Gill denies that these are persons in office, neither ancient widows with some care of the poor nor presbyteresses, as some call them, but godly women in years; Clarke says he believes elderly women are meant and not deaconesses; Barnes will not draw the line so tightly, taking in not only those who may hold the office of deaconess but all aged females. Ellicott sets the charge in a larger frame, that Paul is faithful here to what had become one of the guiding principles of Christianity, the equal position of women as fellow-heirs in the city which hath foundations, and reminds the elder women of Crete that the position Christ and his disciples had claimed for them was not without grave responsibilities. On the demeanour asked of them, he presses that the word covers dress, appearance, conversation and manner alike, an outward deportment dependent on something more internal, so that the younger and more thoughtless sister could respect and reverence it as an ideal she might hope one day to reach. Robertson glosses the same word as of people engaged in sacred duties, and notes that the compound rendered teachers of good things is found nowhere else — a sorely needed mission, he calls it.

On wine the comment turns classical. Clarke observes that both among the Greeks and Romans old women were reputed fond of much wine, citing the ancient scholiast on Homer for the saying that at this age they delight in wine and Ovid for what looks like a literal translation of it, and takes the participle to mean not enslaved by much wine, habit being a species of slavery. Ellicott refers the warning instead to the evil habits and customs of the Cretans. Clarke then presses the connection into the next verse with Jerome's question, how an elderly woman can teach young women chastity when, if the young woman should imitate the drunkenness of the matron, it would be impossible for her to be chaste. Ellicott explains why this teaching was left to the women rather than to Titus: such a reformation in individual life would never be brought about by a sermon or by many sermons however eloquent, but would follow from patient individual effort and holy example. He reads the Cretan disease as a feverish longing for excitement and novelty, women as well as men preferring the tithing of mint and anise and cummin to quietly doing their Father's business, and Paul's correction as a recall to the steady performance of the quiet every-day duties to which God had called them.

Barnes makes the domestic charge carry the weight of the argument, comparing a precept of the Pythagoreans and insisting that no wealth or splendour, no magnificence of entertainment or sweetness of music, can compensate for the want of mutual affection, which will diffuse comfort through the obscurest cottage of poverty. He is careful that keeping at home does not mean never going abroad, only that domestic affairs not be neglected and that a wife not be better known abroad than at home. Henry puts the same warning more sharply, pairing chaste with keepers at home and recalling that Dinah lost her chastity when she went to see the daughters of the land, while allowing that occasions for going abroad exist and naming the real evil as a gadding temper for merriment and company's sake; those whose home is their prison, he adds, may be feared to find their chastity their fetters. Both he and Ellicott end where Paul does, on the enemy who is ever watching, and Clarke supplies the taunt itself: behold your boasted religion, our heathenism is as good as your Christianity.
6:
One word is all the young men get, and the commentators spend their effort explaining why it is enough. Barnes takes it as a well-governed mind, superior to the indulgence of those passions to which the young are prone, and gives five reasons the charge is pressed on them in particular: the hopes of the church depend much on them, a young man who cannot govern himself gives little promise of being useful or happy, indulgence sooner or later brings ruin to body and soul alike, they stand at the period of life most exposed to peculiar temptations, and they may soon die and should be habitually ready to stand before God. Ellicott explains instead why the task falls to Titus, who in respect of age must still be reckoned among them — brought up in a Pagan home, not improbably in luxurious and wicked Syrian Antioch, drawn to the Master's side in the fresh dawn of manhood and tried in many a difficult task, he was about forty when placed over the Cretan Church, and no one could set the peril and its remedy more vividly before them. Ellicott quotes Chrysostom to the effect that no task is after all so hard for youth as obtaining the mastery over oneself in the matter of harmful pleasures. Clarke puts the order of reformation the other way about: it should begin with the old, who have the authority and should give the example, though the young of both sexes must also give account of themselves to God. Henry names the besetting sin exactly — there are more young people ruined by pride than by any other sin — and asks of them the seriousness of age joined with the liveliness and vigour of youth.

The charge then turns on Titus himself, and the phrase in all things is disputed. Robertson allows that it may be taken with sober-minded, though the editors take it with what follows; Clarke refers it not to conduct generally but to the classes just named, so that Titus is to be a pattern to each of them, being in sobriety and gravity and temperance what he requires others to be; Ellicott makes it broadest of all, a ceaseless activity prescribed to the superintending presbyter, setting the pattern now of useful labour and now of brave patient endurance, in peaceful quiet days as in times of danger. Henry states the principle underneath: preachers of good works must be patterns of them also, since without this Titus would pull down with one hand what he built with the other. On the words that follow, Ellicott insists that neither uncorruptness nor gravity refers to the subject-matter of the teaching but to the bearing of the teacher, who must be above seeking popular applause and must keep his gravity in private intercourse with his flock and not only in the delivery of sermons. Barnes and Ellicott both report that sincerity is wanting in the older copies, Barnes naming the editors who reject it; Robertson notes that uncorruptness is the only example of its word in the New Testament.

Sound speech is read by its metaphor. Barnes takes the adjective in its ordinary medical sense of healthful or whole, observing that in this figurative use it belongs in the New Testament to Paul alone. Clarke presses the figure further: human nature is in a state of disease, all false doctrines leave men under its influence, and the unadulterated doctrine of the Gospel alone can heal them. On the closing clause, Clarke reports that a large body of copies and versions read of us rather than of you and calls that reading undoubtedly genuine; Ellicott agrees the older authorities support it, and draws the consequence, that what might have been said against Titus would in reality be spoken against Paul and the elder Apostles.
9:
Whether these words are addressed to slaves or to servants generally decides how the passage reads, and the voices divide. Ellicott insists the accurate translation is bond servants and that the words are addressed to slaves, a large class among whom many Christians were to be found, massed here under one head; Robertson glosses the noun simply as slaves. Clarke agrees they were the property of their masters and adds the sting, that these are exhorted to obey their own despots though those had no right over them on the ground of natural justice. Barnes takes the other line, holding that everything said here would be equally appropriate whether the servitude was voluntary or involuntary, and reading the case of the free man as a contract: he binds himself to obey cheerfully and quietly, not to reason with his employer or instruct him, even though his own opinions may be much wiser. Ellicott suspects the charge was called out by particular instances of insubordination and impatience among the Cretan slaves, and states frankly what the difficulty was — that Christianity had the hard task of persuading the bondman, fellow-heir of heaven with the freeman, that the Master who promised him a home among the many mansions did not mean the existing framework of society to be changed at once.

The limits of obedience are agreed. Barnes allows pleasing the master only so far as one lawfully may, never in anything contrary to the will of God or morally wrong; Gill says in all things that are not contrary to a good conscience, to the Christian religion, and to the laws of God and nature. Gill then offers a second rendering of the same clause which nobody else entertains, that they may be well pleased in all things — that is, satisfied and contented with their state and condition, cheerfully abiding in the calling wherein they are called. On the phrase translated answering again, Clarke, Ellicott and Robertson agree the sense is not gainsaying, and Ellicott adds the tone: obedience without sullenness, not thwarting or setting themselves against their masters' plans. Henry states the whole duty by its motive, that in serving an earthly master according to Christ's will Christ himself is served, and warns against the reflex of guilt — when conscious of a fault, to excuse or justify it doubles it.

On purloining the comment turns evidential. Clarke shows how ordinary the vice was thought by assembling the Latin usage in which the word for a thief simply meant a servant: he quotes the line from Virgil's third eclogue asking what masters may do when servants dare such things, the note of Servius that the word for thief stands for a servant because thefts are peculiarly theirs, the taunt in Plautus that a man is one of three letters, and Terence's phrase for a company of servants as a bundle of thieves. Barnes and Robertson keep to the word itself, the same one used of Ananias and Sapphira keeping back part of the price. Ellicott supplies the opportunity rather than the reputation, since many slaves in the empire were employed beyond house and farm, some entrusted with shops and left quite to themselves, others elaborately trained and working as artists or even physicians, so that a slave had a hundred ways of showing true fidelity as against assumed surface obedience. All four then read the last clause the same way, and the ornament is the point. Robertson observes that Paul is showing slaves how they may adorn the teaching of God; Ellicott quotes Calvin's remark that it is noteworthy how God deigns to receive an adornment from those ranked as possessions, just like cattle or horses; and Barnes turns it upward, that a master should feel the obligation not to be surpassed in religious character by his servant.
11:
Chrysostom reads the conjunction backwards into the slaves' charge: having demanded from servants so great a virtue as adorning the doctrine in all things, Paul adds the just cause why servants should be such: those who have God for their Teacher may well be so, seeing their numberless sins have been forgiven them, and nothing so awes and humbles the soul as to have had innumerable sins to answer for and to have received not punishment but pardon and infinite favours. Henry makes the same link general rather than particular: let young and old, men and women, masters and servants and Titus himself all do their respective duties, for this is the very aim and business of Christianity, and grace is obliging and constraining to goodness, without which effect it is received in vain. He presses that the appearing is a matter of degree and of reach — the old dispensation was comparatively dark and shadowy, this a clear and shining light, and not to the Jews only, as the glory appeared at mount Sinai out of the view of all others, since the pale is now broken down.

What appeared, and to whom, divides them sharply. Gill will not let the phrase mean the free favour in God's own heart, nor the grace wrought in believers' hearts, on the ground that neither of these has ever appeared to all men, and settles instead on the doctrine of grace, the Gospel so called because it is a declaration of grace. Barnes reports both constructions, prefers the marginal one as most in accordance with the Greek, and holds the sense not essentially varied: the plan was fitted for man as man, and might include servants as well as masters, the poor as well as the rich. Ellicott renders it as grace appearing and bringing salvation, and then guards it, calling the phrase one of those hard sayings pressed into the service of a kindly but erring school of expositors who shut their eyes to the warnings addressed to the impenitent; grace alone brings salvation to all men, which asserts not that all will be saved but that it is the only means by which salvation is possible. Clarke goes the other way and builds the whole comment on a figure. The verb has shined out, taken from the sun, and as light and heat are denied to no nation nor individual, so from the influences of this spiritual Sun no soul is reprobated any more than from the natural one, only those being deprived who wilfully shut their eyes. That whole nations have not yet received the light is no objection, since the earth comes into the solar light successively, by its daily turning and by its passage through all the signs of the zodiac, and only when its year is completed has every part its due proportion; and men are not in total darkness before the Gospel reaches them, light having been created three whole days before the sun was formed.

On the teaching itself the divisions are smaller. Clarke takes the participle as instructing us as children are instructed, so that men must become disciples and learn of the great Teacher; Ellicott makes it sterner, disciplining and educating us by life's sad experiences. Gill restricts the pupils to those taught not doctrinally only but with efficacy, since many who profess the Gospel are never influentially taught by it, having a form of godliness but denying its power; Wesley opens it to all who do not reject it, and takes sobriety in the scripture sense to be the whole temper of a man rather than a single virtue. All four then read the three adverbs as one scheme of duty, to ourselves and our neighbour and our God, and Ellicott alone carries the last phrase forward, hearing in the present course of things the reminder that another is at hand.
13:
The first question is whether one thing is being looked for or two. Clarke takes the minority side plainly: some think the blessed hope and the glorious appearing mean the same thing, but he does not, referring the hope to eternal glorification in general and the appearing to the resurrection of the body, when Christ shall change this vile body and make it like his own. Ellicott renders the clause as a single object, the blessed hope and manifestation of the glory, and binds the two together: the hope is the hope of glory we shall share with the Son when we behold him as he is, so that the life of the lover of the Lord must be one continued waiting for that hour. Gill rejects the first candidate, since the grace of hope is already implanted in regeneration and cannot be said to be looked for; he allows that Christ himself may be meant, but since Christ is named in the next clause he prefers the thing hoped for, the eternal glory that will lie in the beatific vision. Robertson notes that the participle is the one used of those who were looking for the Messiah, and that the noun means the second epiphany where elsewhere it means the first. Cyril, expounding the two comings, sets Malachi over the passage: the Lord whom ye seek shall suddenly come to his temple; and of the second, who shall abide the day of his coming, for he cometh like a refiner's fire.

On the great God the voices are one, and it is the fullest textual argument in the chapter. Barnes says there can be little doubt the apostle meant the Lord Jesus, since the coming of God as such is nowhere taught and the phrase is applied in the New Testament to no other; if Paul did not mean this, he adds, he used language fitted to lead men into error. He lists the names by which the reading has been vindicated, Beza and Whitby and Bull and Matthaei and Middleton on the Greek article. Ellicott grants that on grammatical principles either translation would be possible, then piles up what is not balanced: the word for manifestation is used by Paul five times and always of Christ, never of the Father, and an epiphany of the Father would be an idea strange to the New Testament and dropped as soon as suggested. His weightiest argument is the consensus of the Greek fathers, and he quotes two: Theodoret, that Paul here calls Christ the great God and so rebukes the blasphemy which denies his Godhead, and Chrysostom's question, what those can say who allege the Son is inferior to the Father. Robertson makes it shorter: one article with both nouns gives the necessary meaning. Clarke, translating it as the appearing of the glory of the great God, even our Saviour Jesus Christ, sends the reader to an essay on the Greek article.

The last verse divides them again over one word. Barnes will not let a peculiar people mean unlike others, however true that may be otherwise; the term means belonging to Christ rather than to ourselves, his own as a man's property is his own, and the passage should not be used to prove a distinctive manner of living. Ellicott reads the contrast as the whole point, tracing the phrase to the Greek Old Testament and to the people Jehovah would have peculiarly his own, set apart from a mankind lawless and idolatrous, as Jesus would set apart a people out of a humanity sunk in selfish sins. Clarke turns it into a manumission: having purchased the slaves from their thraldom he strips them of their sordid vestments and cleanses them, bringing them out of a servitude in which they had no motive to diligence and no affection for the despot over them, so that they become willing servants.
15:
The closing verse is read as a summary of the chapter and then as a charge about Titus himself. Henry divides it into matter and manner: the matter is these things, not Jewish fables and traditions but the truths and duties just set out, so that ministers in preaching must keep close to the word of God and not the figments and inventions of their own brain; the manner is doctrine and exhortation and reproof together, and the exhortation is to be pressed with much earnestness, since ministers must not be cold and lifeless in delivering heavenly doctrine as if it were of little concern. Clarke glosses the three verbs in turn, noting that the first means teach and that one manuscript actually reads the ordinary word for teaching, that the second is to repeat them again and again and urge them on the conscience, and that the third is to demonstrate their necessity and show that God requires obedience. Barnes takes the noun rendered authority to mean command, so that Titus was to speak decidedly, without ambiguity and without compromise, stating these things not as advice or counsel but as the requirement of God. Ellicott sets the verse as the close of a division of the letter, and hears in it the voice of the brave-hearted old man telling his disciple to speak with decision and to rebuke, if need be, with vigour, remembering the dark character of the people with whom he had to do.

The last clause divides them. Barnes, Clarke and Ellicott read it as a charge on Titus' own conduct — act so that no person shall have cause to despise thee, either for thy work or for the manner and spirit in which thou dost perform it, so that every word of thine may have its full weight. Henry gives that reading too, adding that the most effectual way for ministers to secure themselves from contempt is to preach and live well and do their duty with prudence and courage, and that he who despises despises not man but God; but he alone suggests a second addressee, that an admonition might here be intended for the people as well, that Titus, though young and but a substitute of the apostle, should be considered and respected and supported in his work. Robertson finds the point in the verb, which is not the stronger word of scorn used elsewhere but one meaning to think around on all sides, so that the prohibition is literally that no man think around thee — the possibility being of someone making mental circles about a minister and so out-thinking him; from which he draws the plain conclusion that the best way to command respect for one's authority is to do thinking that will deserve it.

Clarke ends by standing back from the whole chapter, and few portions of the New Testament, he says, excel it: it may well form the creed and system of ethics and text book of every Christian preacher, since it sets out what he is to believe, what to practise and what to preach, and even parcels out his congregation to him, the old and young of both sexes and those in their employment. He draws four things from it in order — the duty of a Gospel minister, the Godhead of Christ stated so explicitly that the expressions cannot be misapplied, the extent of redemption with none passed by and none left without the first offer of life eternal, and the operation of grace in cleansing and purifying the soul for glory — then turns on his reader with the warning that neglect in such a case is the highest contempt a man can offer his Maker.
